what: Peaucellier–Lipkin inversor: an exact straight-line linkage. From a fixed pivot O two 64 mm arms run to the side corners B and D of a rhombus of four 48 mm beams; its other corners are P and the output point Q. Motor A turns a 16 mm crank about an axis 16 mm from O, so P moves on a circle that passes through O. The red output marker at Q has no guide; the white rail 16 mm beside its path is only a visual reference and is not connected to it. The program sweeps the crank slowly to +60°, home, −60° and home (15°/s with 3 s pauses), repeats the sweep at 30°/s, and ends at home. Experimental model: the law described here has so far been measured only in the simulator (one headless run), not on real LEGO parts.
try: Reset. At home, note where the red output marker sits opposite the white reference rail.
During the slow sweep to +60°, watch the gap between the marker and the rail. In the ideal geometry it stays 16 mm all the way.
Compare how far the marker moves for the same crank rotation near home and near the ends of the sweep. Are the distances equal?
Compare the slow sweeps with the faster repetition: the marker should trace the same line at both speeds.
why: The rhombus cell is a circle inverter. Because OB = OD and all four rhombus sides are equal, O, P and Q always lie on one line, and OP × OQ = OB² − BP² = 64² − 48² = 1792 mm², a constant. Inversion turns every circle through O into a straight line. P is held on such a circle (a 16 mm crank about a centre 16 mm from O), so Q must lie on the line perpendicular to the crank’s frame line at 1792 / (2 × 16) = 56 mm from O. With crank angle φ, Q moves along that line by y = 56 mm × tan(φ/2): ±32.3 mm at ±60°, a total stroke of about 64.7 mm. In the simulator, the measured output point stayed within 0.16 mm of a straight line (56.0–56.3 mm from O) over the whole run and within 0.24 mm of 56 mm × tan(φ/2).
matters: Before precise slideways could be machined, engineers needed straight motion from pivots alone. Watt’s linkage gives only an approximate line; Peaucellier’s inversor (1864, found independently by Lipkin) was the first planar linkage to give an exact one. It also shows that a mechanism can compute a geometric transformation. Exactness belongs to the ideal geometry: real pins with clearance and flexing beams deviate slightly, and the simulator has small solver errors of its own.
question: The crank turns in equal steps at constant speed. Does the output marker move in equal steps along its line? And why does the program stop at ±60° instead of turning the crank all the way round?
answer: No: y = 56 mm × tan(φ/2) grows faster towards the ends. The first 15° from home moves Q about 7.4 mm, the step from 45° to 60° about 9.1 mm. A full turn is impossible: the cell is fully stretched when OQ = 64 + 48 = 112 mm, which happens at φ = ±120°. Beyond that no position of the links exists, so the program stays well inside at ±60°.
further: Calculate y at each 15° step from 0° to 60° and compare it with the marker. The gap to the rail should stay 16 mm.
On paper, make all four rhombus sides 40 mm: the constant becomes 64² − 40² = 2496 mm² and the line moves to 78 mm from O – still exactly straight.

Compare Watt’s Line (approximate straight line) and Straight Eight, an established Peaucellier–Lipkin model. Here straightness comes only from geometry: there is no slider or software constraint on Q.
formula: OP × OQ = OB² − BP² = 64² − 48² = 1792 mm². P on a circle of radius r = 16 mm through O → Q on the line x = (OB² − BP²) / (2r) = 56 mm. y_Q = 56 mm × tan(φ/2): ±32.3 mm at φ = ±60°. Full stretch at OQ = 112 mm ↔ φ = ±120°.
